of God in Nature.’ (Coleridge, Poetical Works, ed. J. C. C. Mays (2001) i, Pt I, 464) Given its
Italian orientation, it is likely that Vittorio Alfieri’s writings critiquing tyranny, particularly in
the context of late-eighteenth-century Italy and France, inform S.’s sonnet. In his essay Della
Tirannide (1787), Alfieri condemns political servitude of the kind S. identifies with Sgricci:
‘in a tyranny only those few deserve to be slaves who, though possessing the idea of liberty
(and consequently the strength or the skill to try at least to regain it for themselves, and at the
same time for others), yet prefer to live in servitude’ (trans. Julius A. Molinaro and Beatrice
Corrigan (1961) 93). S. would also have been familiar with the way that Staël draws attention

paragraphs.source_en:
Nous sommes esclaves, mais des esclaves toujours frémissants, dit Alfiéri, le plus fier de
nos écrivains modernes. Il y a tant d’ame dans nos beaux arts, que peut-être un jour
notre caractère égalera notre génie.
 (Ed. Simone Balayé (1985) 104)
